traveler: Count Orlando di Chiusi in Casentino (Orlando Cattani / di Catenaia)
title: The Sentence at the Table: the Count of Chiusi and the Gift of La Verna
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the fief granted to the house of Catenaia
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna' records the 967 investiture of Goffredo del fu Ildebrando di Catenaia by Otto I
stops.campa: In 967 the emperor Otto I invests Goffredo, son of the late Ildebrando di Catenaia, with the land under the mountain in the upper Casentino. A castle goes up on the terminal spur of Monte della Verna, above the oldest roofs of the town, and the wooded height at its back is held the way any lord holds a stand of timber and wolf-ground. Two and a half centuries of tenure follow. The count who will one day give that mountain away inherits the rock and a name the sources spell two ways. The Aretine documents write the family di Catenaia; the Franciscan books write Cattani.
suggested_refs: The Cassero of Chiusi della Verna, on the southern spur of the mountain

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, a birth with no year
stops.date_confidence: unattested: no source consulted gives a birth date, year, or parentage; 1180 is a placeholder for a man already adult and titled in 1213
stops.campa: No register, no chronicle, no notarial hand records when he is born or to whom. He enters the record already grown and already titled: il conte Orlando di Chiusi in Casentino. Where the Franciscan books would need a father they supply none, and the Aretine sources that know his family know it as a lineage rather than as a set of lives. The Treccani biographical dictionary returns no retrievable entry. What can be said is the ground: a castle at the southern end of the mountain, a town beneath it, a fief the bishops of Arezzo will one day want back. Whether he is thirty in 1213 or sixty, no source consulted allows a guess.
suggested_refs: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (no retrievable entry for Orlando di Chiusi)

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, four names for one man
stops.date_confidence: gap: no standardized modern form of the name exists; the variants are given as found and not reconciled
stops.campa: The books call him Orlando Cattani da Chiusi, and Orlando Catani, and Orlando di Catenaia, and simply il conte Orlando di Chiusi in Casentino. The Franciscan tradition prefers Cattani; the article on his own castle uses it too, calling the ruin the rocca of Count Orlando Cattani. The Aretine record of the fief calls the family di Catenaia. Cattani may be Catenaia worn down by four centuries of copying, or it may not be, and no source consulted asserts the connection. No modern biographical dictionary entry could be retrieved to fix which form is right.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'Cassero (Chiusi della Verna)', which names the ruin for Count Orlando Cattani

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the mountain before it is given
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the mountain's tenure with the fief of Chiusi is attested; no source dates Orlando's own use of it
stops.campa: A mile north of his castle the ground climbs into cliff and beech forest, cut by ravines, broken by an overhanging rock that roofs a dry space beneath it, watered by a spring. Wolves range the slopes and falcons nest on the crags. It is a great deal of country worth very little: too steep to plough, too high to settle, useful to a count chiefly as timber and hunting. Orlando holds it as any lord holds the least productive corner of what he owns. In 1213 there is nothing on the shelf under the summit but beech, rock and running water.
suggested_refs: The forest, cliffs, spring and Sasso Spicco of Monte della Verna, upper Casentino

stops.name: San Leo, the rocca on the crag
stops.date_confidence: traditional: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' attests the meeting at San Leo in spring 1213; the knighting feast comes only from the First Consideration, and the day 8 May from later devotional tradition
stops.campa: The Montefeltro capital stands on a single rock with vertical sides, reached by one cut road. A knighting is held in the fortress and the lords of the country ride up for it, Orlando among them, out of Tuscany and over the Apennine watershed into Romagna. He has heard of the friar from Assisi and wants to hear him preach. Everything that happens at that feast reaches us through the devotional books alone. Of the year 1213 the civic history of San Leo records one line, that Francis passed through. It mentions no feast, no count and no gift.
stops.quote: He was called Orlando da Chiusi di Casentino; and for the marvellous things which he had heard concerning the holiness and the miracles of St Francis he bore him great devotion, and had an exceeding desire to see him and to hear him preach.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition, trans. rev. Dom Roger Hudleston, O.S.B.)
suggested_refs: The rocca of San Leo, historic capital of the Montefeltro
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: San Leo, the sermon on the low wall
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sermon on the wall is narrated only in the First Consideration, a fourteenth-century devotional text
stops.campa: Francis climbs onto a low wall in the courtyard where the company is gathered and preaches on two lines of vernacular verse, a couplet in the meter of love songs turned to another use. The words are about pain and joy, in the language Orlando would have heard sung at any other table in the Casentino. He is standing in the crowd of a feast he came to as a neighbour and a guest, among men who have ridden up for a knighting. The tradition says not one of the knights present leaves off listening while Francis is on the wall.
stops.quote: So great is the joy which I expect, That all pain is joy to me.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition); the same couplet appears in this atlas's file for Francis in another translation, as So great is the good I have in sight, that every pain to me is a delight
suggested_refs: The courtyard wall of the rocca of San Leo, site of the sermon in the First Consideration
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: San Leo, drawn aside from the table
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: When the preaching ends the count does not go back to the company. He comes to Francis and asks for counsel about the salvation of his soul, in the words the Considerations put in his mouth. It is a formula, and it is also the whole of what survives of his interior life: one sentence, asked standing, at a party. A lord in his prime asks a beggar for advice in front of an armed hall and the text finds nothing remarkable in it. What was he afraid of, what had he done, what did he want absolved? The record does not answer any of the three.
stops.quote: O Father, I would fain take counsel with thee concerning the salvation of my soul.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition)
suggested_refs: Ferdinando Folchi, canvas of the meeting of Francis and Count Orlando Catani at San Leo (1877), La Verna
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: San Leo, sent back to his friends
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Francis will not take a man out of his obligations, not even toward himself. Orlando is a guest at another lord's knighting, and a guest owes the table its hours. So the count goes back to the company and eats, and the conversation that will hand over a mountain waits until the plates are cleared. This is the only extended exchange between the two men that any source reports, and its subject is who is owed the afternoon. Nothing in the text suggests either of them is in a hurry.
stops.quote: It pleaseth me well: but go now and pay respect to thy friends, who have bidden thee to this feast, and dine with them; and after dinner we will speak together as much as it shall please thee.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition)
suggested_refs: The great hall of the rocca of San Leo
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: San Leo, the mountain offered
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the offer is preserved in the First Consideration and quoted in Italian by it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna'; no charter or notarial instrument survives
stops.campa: After dinner he makes the offer. The Italian of the Fioretti keeps it as Io ho in Toscana uno monte divotissimo il quale si chiama monte della Vernia, a most devout mountain: the adjective belongs to the place before any friar has prayed on it. He asks no rent, no service, no reservation of the timber or the hunting. The consideration named is the welfare of his own soul. The whole conveyance is one sentence spoken at a table in the Montefeltro. No charter is drawn and no notary is called.
stops.quote: I have a mountain in Tuscany, a devout and solitary place, called Mount Alvernia, far from all discourse of men, well fitted for one who would do penance for his sins, or who desires to lead a solitary life; if it please thee, I will freely give it to thee and thy companions for the welfare of my soul.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition)
suggested_refs: The Italian text of the offer as quoted in it.wikipedia, 'Santuario della Verna'
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: San Leo, the condition of acceptance
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Francis does not accept on the spot. He will send brothers to look, and if they find the place fit for prayer and penance he will take it. The count is to receive them and show them the ground. It is the answer of a man who has been offered property before and knows what most of it is worth for his purpose. So the gift stands provisional for the length of a journey across the mountains and back, and two friars will decide whether a mountain changes hands.
stops.quote: Orlando, as soon as thou shalt have returned to thy home, I will send to thee some of our brethren, to whom thou shalt show this place; and if it shall seem to them well fitted for prayer and penance, I will at once accept thy charitable offer.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition)
suggested_refs: The 1274 instrument of the donation of La Verna, cited in this atlas's file for Francis of Assisi
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: San Leo, the day the tradition fixes
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged: it.wikipedia dates the encounter to spring 1213; the CCEL text of the First Consideration names the place only as the Castle of Montefeltro and sets the episode in 1224; 8 May 1213 is traditional, carried by Folchi's 1877 canvas and repeated by en.wikipedia. Not resolved.
stops.campa: The books do not agree about this day. The Italian tradition puts the meeting in the spring of 1213. The English text of the First Consideration names the place only as the castle of Montefeltro and sets the whole episode in 1224, the year of the stigmata, eleven years late. The date 8 May survives chiefly because a painter lettered it under a canvas in 1877. There is no instrument, no seal, no dated act. Which year is right cannot be settled from the sources consulted here.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'San Leo (Italia)': Fu luogo di passaggio di san Francesco nel 1213
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

segments.name: The Road Home and the Fifty Men-at-Arms

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the count comes home
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the return follows the San Leo meeting in the narrative sequence of the First Consideration; no source dates it
stops.campa: He rides back over the passes to his own rock. The text is careful about the distance, about a mile between the castle and the mountain, and the distance is the point: what he has given away stands in sight of his windows. From the spur where the Cassero sits he can look up the slope at property that is no longer his. No one has gone up yet, and nothing at the castle has been told to change. The beech wood on the height looks in June exactly as it looked in April.
stops.quote: And Orlando likewise returned to his castle, which was called Chiusi, and was about a mile distant from Mount Alvernia.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition)
suggested_refs: The Cassero of Chiusi della Verna, above the oldest quarter of the town
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the two brothers received
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the reception and the escort are narrated in the First Consideration; no charter or chronicle corroborates them
stops.campa: Two friars arrive at the castle as promised and the count keeps his end. He feeds them, lodges them, and then does the one thing a lord can do that a mendicant cannot. He puts fifty armed men at their backs for the climb, against the wolves. The ground they are to inspect begins a mile north of his gate. It is the only act of Orlando's that the tradition describes in any operational detail. Fifty men-at-arms come out of a fighting household for two friars walking up a hill a mile away.
stops.quote: St Francis then sent two of his companions to the said Orlando, who received them with much charity and gladness; and he sent with them to Mount Alvernia fully fifty men-at-arms, to be their defence against wild beasts.
stops.quote_source: The Little Flowers of St Francis, Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL edition)
suggested_refs: The castle hall of Chiusi, where the First Consideration places the reception of the two friars
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: The road from Chiusi to the mountain, the escort climbing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the route between castle and mountain is fixed geography; no source narrates the ascent itself, and none places Orlando on it
stops.campa: The way runs north out of the town and climbs some four hundred metres through beech and fir to the shelf under the summit. Fifty men-at-arms go with two friars in habits, an escort out of all proportion to the errand and exactly proportionate to the wolves. Nothing in the record says Orlando rides with them; the tradition leaves him at the castle. The men who climb are his, the wood they climb through is his, and the inspection is of his own gift. Not one of the fifty is named.
suggested_refs: The old track from Chiusi della Verna up to the sanctuary shelf
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the friars find it as he described
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: They come out on the shelf under the crags and find what he told them at San Leo: a place remote from all discourse of men, forested, cliff-broken, with water. Falcons are on the rock. They are the first men sent up the mountain on Francis's account, and they are looking at it as surveyors rather than as hermits. Their report goes back down the valley and the provisional gift becomes a real one. Two men were sent to look at a wood and have come back saying the wood will do. The Franciscan order will still hold the mountain eight hundred years later.
suggested_refs: The spring on the sanctuary shelf of La Verna
sources: Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration (CCEL)

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the first hermits on the shelf
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' has Francis and companions occupying the mountain after the donation; the month is not fixed in any source
stops.campa: Francis and a few companions come up and take possession, if that word fits men who own nothing. They live on the shelf intermittently, going away and returning, using it as the count described it: a place for whoever wishes to do penance far from mankind. The English tradition is careful about the terms. The mountain is given to Francis personally, for solitary penance, and not to the order as an institution, which makes it a private arrangement between a Casentine lord and a man with no property. What the count understood himself to be giving away is not recorded.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'La Verna', on the donation as a personal rather than institutional gift

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the Sasso Spicco
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' places the first cell of wood and earth near the Sasso Spicco; the year is not fixed and Orlando is not placed there by any source
stops.campa: Below the shelf the rock overhangs in a great cleft, a roofed emptiness of stone with water running somewhere under it. Near this the first cell is raised, of wood and earth. It stands on donated ground, and nobody has drawn a boundary inside the donation: the mountain went whole, cliffs, spring, cleft, timber, wolves and all. Orlando's title to every part of it ended at San Leo with one spoken sentence. No source puts the count under this rock at any time in his life.
suggested_refs: The Sasso Spicco, below the sanctuary of La Verna, reached from the Corridoio delle Stimmate

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the chapel of Santa Maria degli Angeli begun
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' dates the construction 1216-1218; en.wikipedia 'La Verna' credits Orlando with helping to finance it
stops.campa: The friars begin a church on the shelf. The tradition holds that the Virgin of the Angels appeared to Francis in a dream and indicated both the site and the dimensions, so that the building goes up to a measure received asleep. Orlando helps to pay for it. The mountain he gave away in a sentence he now underwrites in stone, lime and wages. Both Wikipedias trace the funding to the same sanctuary tradition, and no account book survives to show what he spent.
suggested_refs: The chapel of Santa Maria degli Angeli, La Verna, first permanent building on the mountain

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the chapel finished
stops.date_confidence: attested: construction 1216-1218 per it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna'
stops.campa: In 1218 the little church stands, the first permanent building on the mountain, dedicated by Francis's own will to the Virgin of the Angels. It went up between 1216 and 1218, the first work in stone on a height that had carried nothing but a cell of wood and earth. Five years earlier the ground held wolves and a spring and nothing else. The count of Chiusi has now given away a mountain and paid toward a church on it, and those two acts are his entire documented career. After 1218 the sources lose him for forty-three years.
suggested_refs: The dedication of the first chapel of La Verna to the Virgin of the Angels

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the years without record
stops.date_confidence: gap: no source consulted places Orlando anywhere, or records any act of his, between 1218 and the Aretine notice of 1261
stops.campa: For four decades the man is missing from his own story. No second meeting with Francis is recorded, no visit to the mountain, no letter, no lawsuit, no witness list, no oath. He goes on presumably doing what a count of Chiusi does, holding a castle, judging his men, taking what the fief renders. The Franciscan writers have no further use for him once the mountain is theirs, and the Aretine notaries have not yet had cause to write his name. Between 1218 and 1261 he appears in nothing that has been found.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'Cassero (Chiusi della Verna)', which states that no historical documentation of Orlando survives beyond the donation legend

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the stigmata on his ground
stops.date_confidence: traditional; contradiction flagged: en.wikipedia 'La Verna' and this atlas's file for Francis give 14 September, the Exaltation of the Cross, while it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' gives 17 September, the feast of the Impression of the Stigmata. Not resolved.
stops.campa: Eleven years after the sentence at the table, Francis keeps a forty-day fast on the mountain with Brother Leo and three companions and takes on his body the five wounds. It happens on land a Casentine count gave away without a notary and without witnesses, for the welfare of his soul. The sources put nobody from Chiusi on the shelf that September. The chapel that will mark the place is not raised for another thirty-nine years, and a different family pays for it.
suggested_refs: The Cappella delle Stimmate, La Verna, built 1263 at the expense of Count Simone Guidi da Battifolle
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'La Verna, the seraph and the stigmata'

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, whether the news came down
stops.date_confidence: gap: no source records that Orlando learned of the stigmata, when he learned, or what he said; nothing here is asserted beyond the silence
stops.campa: A mile below the shelf stands a castle. Nothing in any source consulted says that word came down to it, or that the count went up, or that anyone thought to tell him. He is the nearest lord and the donor of the ground and the record does not give him a sentence. The silence is not evidence that he was indifferent and it is not evidence that he was moved. Did anyone at Chiusi hear of it that autumn? The books that tell the story of the wounds do not think to say.
sources: Gap noted across it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna', it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna', en.wikipedia 'La Verna', en.wikipedia 'Francis of Assisi'

segments.name: The Name in the Aretine Record

stops.name: La Verna, the church he paid for outgrown
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' dates the consecration of the enlarged church to 1260
stops.campa: The chapel of 1216 is no longer large enough for the traffic the stigmata bring. The friars enlarge it, and in 1260 the enlarged church is consecrated with bishops present. The shell Orlando's money raised survives inside a bigger building, which is what usually happens to a founder's church. What the sanctuary keeps of him instead is a story about a feast and a sentence. There is no inscription with his name on it, no arms over a door, and no record of a mass said for him at the consecration.
suggested_refs: The tramezzo and enlarged nave of Santa Maria degli Angeli, La Verna

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, sovereignty claimed over the fief
stops.date_confidence: attested for the act, unresolved for the man: it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna' names the three brothers; whether this Orlando is the count of 1213, then very old, or a descendant of the same name, no source says
stops.campa: Guglielmino degli Ubertini, bishop of Arezzo, asserts his own sovereignty over the fief and leaves the brothers Orlando, Alberto and Niccolo di Catenaia lordship over the castle of Chiusi alone. The house keeps its rock and loses the country around it. Forty-eight years separate this Orlando from the one who rode to San Leo. He may be the same man grown very old; he may be a grandson wearing the name. The source does not say and this account does not decide.
suggested_refs: it.wikipedia, 'Chiusi della Verna': lasciando ai fratelli Orlando, Alberto e Niccolo di Catenaia il solo dominio sul castello di Chiusi

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, the death with no date
stops.date_confidence: unattested: no source consulted gives a date, place or circumstance of death; 1270 is a placeholder and carries no evidential weight
stops.campa: There is no year and no place. No illness, no deathbed, no will. The article on the Cassero says plainly that no historical documentation of Orlando survives beyond the legend of the donation, and nothing found in this research contradicts it. A Treccani biographical entry that might have fixed his dates returned no retrievable text this pass. He is a man known for one afternoon and one building account. The date carried here is a placeholder and carries no evidential weight.
suggested_refs: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (sought, no retrievable entry)

stops.name: Monte della Verna, the instrument of 1274
stops.date_confidence: uncorroborated: the 1274 confirming instrument is cited in this atlas's own file for Francis of Assisi; no source consulted this pass names, dates or reproduces it, and whether Orlando or his heirs acted could not be established
stops.campa: Sixty-one years after the sentence at the table, an instrument confirming the donation of La Verna is drawn up. By then the man who spoke the sentence is presumed dead, and the act is presumed to be his heirs putting a spoken thing into a written one, because the order now needs a document where a count once needed only his word. Neither presumption is proved. No source consulted this pass names the instrument, dates it, or reproduces it, and its existence rests on a single internal citation.
suggested_refs: The 1274 instrument of the donation of La Verna
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, suggested_refs of the San Leo stop

stops.name: Chiusi della Verna, no tomb
stops.date_confidence: gap: no burial place, tomb, epitaph or interment record for Orlando was found in any source consulted; the date is a placeholder
stops.campa: No grave, no epitaph, no slab, no burial record names him, at La Verna or at Chiusi or anywhere else. Local Franciscan memory keeps him as the donor of the mountain and keeps nothing of his body. There is no shrine and no anniversary mass recorded under his name. The sanctuary keeps his name in its account of the donation and keeps nothing else of him. Any future claim of a specific grave for him should be treated with suspicion until a document is produced. Where the count of Chiusi was buried is not known.
sources: Gap noted across it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' and it.wikipedia 'Chiusi della Verna'

stops.name: La Verna, the patronage passes out of the house of Chiusi
stops.date_confidence: attested for each act, per it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' and 'Chiusi della Verna'; the Tarlati chapel is dated only to the end of the fourteenth century, with no year given
stops.campa: Count Simone Guidi da Battifolle pays for the chapel over the place of the stigmata in 1263. Late in the fourteenth century the countess Caterina Tarlati raises a chapel on the site of Francis's first brushwood hut. In 1348 Count Tarlato di Pietramala begins the great church of the Assumption, still unfinished in 1459. None of these are Catenaia. The Tarlati are Aretine lords with no attested descent from the counts of Chiusi, and they enlarge the Cassero at Chiusi as well, taking the castle along with the patronage.
suggested_refs: The Cappella delle Stimmate (1263), the chapel of Santa Maria Maddalena (late 14th c.), and the basilica of the Assumption (begun 1348, completed 1459), La Verna

stops.name: La Verna, the two canvases of 1877
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Santuario della Verna' records due tele del pittore fiorentino Ferdinando Folchi del 1877 on the walls before the tramezzo; the 8 May 1213 caption detail comes from en.wikipedia 'La Verna' only
stops.campa: In 1877 the Florentine painter Ferdinando Folchi delivers two canvases for the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli, hung on the walls of the space in front of the tramezzo. One shows Francis meeting Count Orlando Catani at the fortress of San Leo. The other shows the dedication of the chapel. Under the first the date 8 May 1213 is lettered, six hundred and sixty-four years after nothing was written down. No source records what the count looked like, so the face is Folchi's. The two canvases hang before the tramezzo in the church he helped to pay for.
suggested_refs: Ferdinando Folchi, two canvases of 1877, Santa Maria degli Angeli, La Verna
